summary: Describes a model for operational statistics in the Internet, for use by tools that collect and report on network performance and usage. It is informational and defines a model and protocol, not a standard.

plainLanguage.summary: A shared plan for counting how busy the network is, so different tools can keep tidy and comparable notes.

questions: what is a model for operational statistics
how to measure internet operational statistics
which metrics should a network operator collect
how often should network counters be polled
subtitle: A common recipe for which network counters to collect, how often, how to store them and how to report them.

tldr.problem: Network operators each collected and displayed statistics in their own way, so their numbers could not easily be compared or shared.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC picks a minimal set of SNMP-retrievable metrics, recommends polling them every 60 seconds or a multiple of it, defines a text file format for storing and aggregating the data, and suggests report types.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational model, not a standard, and it replaces RFC 1404. The author calls it a first effort at formalizing a common basis for operational statistics.

today: RFC 1857 is an Informational memo that obsoletes RFC 1404 and has not itself been obsoleted or updated. It describes a model and a file format rather than an Internet standard.

sections.title: The Model and Its Goals
sections.content:
Network administrations collect and archive management metrics to isolate problems and plan growth, and increasingly to cooperate with other networks as the number of Internet service providers grows. But tools measure and present data differently, and there is no agreement on which metrics to collect regularly or how to show them.

RFC 1857 proposes a model with four parts: a minimal set of common metrics, tools to collect them, a common interchange format, and common presentation formats. Collection tools store data in a common statistics database, and presentation tools read it later. Old tools can be retrofitted with conversion filters. The main purpose is to let network operation centers (NOCs) share their statistics, with a baseline that takes minimal effort to support.
sections.plainLanguage: Everyone agrees to count the same things in the same way, so any chart-drawing tool can use anyone's numbers.

sections.title: Which Metrics, and How Often
sections.content:
The RFC groups possible metrics into utilization, performance, availability and stability, then sorts them by how easy they are to retrieve. To keep the baseline simple, it recommends only metrics found in the Internet Standard MIB, readable with SNMP. For each interface these are ifInOctets, ifOutOctets, ifInUcastPkts, ifOutUcastPkts, ifInNUcastPkts, ifOutNUcastPkts, ifInDiscards, ifOutDiscards and ifOperStatus. For each node they are ipForwDatagrams, ipInDiscards and sysUpTime.

To catch peak behavior, the four octet and unicast packet counters should be polled at a maximum period of 1 minute (60 seconds). If that is not possible, use an exact multiple of 60 seconds. The remaining variables can be polled more slowly, with no rate specified but again a multiple of 60 seconds. All polling values are recommendations, not requirements.
sections.plainLanguage: It makes a short shopping list of things to count, like how many messages went in and out, and says to check the busiest counters once a minute.

sections.title: Pre-Processing and Aggregation
sections.content:
Raw data is often reduced before it is stored. If a link is down, there is no need to keep writing a counter that is not changing, and sysUpTime and ifOperStatus make it possible to skip such data. The data should also be tied to the resource of interest, such as a given link, so that changing the interface in a gateway does not show up in the results.

Aggregation replaces values over many time intervals with one value computed over the combined interval. The model uses either the arithmetic mean or the maximum, depending on whether you want to track the average or the peak. It reduces data volume but also reduces the information available. Suggested periods are: over a 24 hour period aggregate to 15 minutes, over a month aggregate to 1 hour, and over a year aggregate to 1 day. Appendix A gives the formulas, for instance 15-minute totals as sums of one-minute polls.
sections.plainLanguage: If you write down your height every day for a year, you may later keep only one note per week. You save space, but you lose some details.

sections.title: The Storage and Interchange Format
sections.content:
The format is an interchange file, not necessarily how data is kept internally. White space is ignored, and text from a hash symbol to the end of the line is ignored. A file is built from three kinds of section. A device section says which network, router and link the data comes from, the bandwidth in bits per second (0 if unknown), the protocol type (IP, DECNET, X.25, CLNS, IPX or AppleTalk), the address, the time zone, and an optional tag table. A label section gives the start and stop times (in UTC) and the tags used, and says where the data is. A data section holds one data field per poll: a timestamp, a tag, the seconds since the previous poll and the values.

A tag ties together variables that share one polling and aggregation period, and has a class: total for original or summed values, or peak for maximums. Counters are stored as delta values, and non-counters such as ifOperStatus as absolute values. Fields may be separated by a comma, semicolon or colon, and lists may be bracketed with parentheses, square brackets or braces.

The RFC estimates one year of storage for the 12 recommended variables at 775 kB, assuming 1-minute data kept 1 day, 15-minute data 1 week, hourly data 1 month and daily data 1 year.
sections.plainLanguage: Each file starts with a label that says where and when the numbers came from, then lists the numbers, so nobody has to repeat the label on every line.

sections.title: Reports
sections.content:
The RFC suggests daily reports for operations, weekly reports for medium-term engineering, and monthly and yearly reports for long-term trends. Reports should cover offered load (total traffic at external interfaces, split by customer, and by protocol or application) and resource utilization for links and routers.

For offered load by link, use a bar chart of input and output octets and packets per external interface. For offered load by customer, sort customers by traffic in decreasing order and plot either the cumulative percentage for the top n customers or the percentage for the nth customer. What counts as a customer is defined locally. For utilization, show the average and the peak in the same bar, like peak meters on audio equipment, or put the ten-minute samples in a histogram.
sections.plainLanguage: The reports are bar charts and graphs, like a scoreboard showing who sent the most and when the busiest moments happened.

sections.title: Security Issues
sections.content: Sharing operational data raises legal, ethical and political concerns. Network service providers in particular worry about showing data that could make one of their networks look bad. The RFC therefore says there is a need to ensure integrity, conformity and confidentiality of shared data, and that the same data should be collected from every site at the same interval to be useful. The formal Security Considerations section just points back to this discussion.
sections.plainLanguage: Nobody wants to show a bad report card to everyone, so people need to trust that shared numbers are correct and kept private.
